proposals.name: Plain-language accessibility
proposals.rationale: Readability broadens the pool of readers able and willing to click.
proposals.description: Scores high when wording is immediately understandable without specialist knowledge, and low when jargon or dense syntax impedes comprehension; does not apply when wording is equally clear either way.

proposals.name: Everyday relatability
proposals.rationale: Self-recognition can motivate readership independently of human-interest framing.
proposals.description: Scores high when readers can readily imagine themselves encountering the situation, and low when it feels remote or unrecognizable; does not apply when no personal experience is implied.

proposals.name: Personal usefulness
proposals.rationale: Practical value can attract clicks even without conventional news prominence.
proposals.description: Scores high when the headline promises advice or information applicable to readers’ decisions, and low when it offers only observation; does not apply without an actionable implication.

proposals.name: Curiosity gap
proposals.rationale: Withheld answers create a direct incentive to open the article.
proposals.description: Scores high when a salient explanation is withheld while an answer is clearly implied, and low when the headline fully resolves its premise; does not apply without a meaningful information gap.

proposals.name: Unresolved outcome
proposals.rationale: Open trajectories encourage readers to seek developments or resolution.
proposals.description: Scores high when an event or process remains visibly undecided, and low when its result is already settled; does not apply to static descriptions without an outcome trajectory.

proposals.name: Emotional arousal
proposals.rationale: Strong affect can drive attention independently of crisis, violence, or human-interest status.
proposals.description: Scores high when wording strongly evokes fear, wonder, anger, joy, or disgust, and low when emotionally neutral; does not apply when affect is genuinely indeterminate.

proposals.name: Moral contestability
proposals.rationale: Moral evaluation can generate readership through disagreement and self-positioning.
proposals.description: Scores high when the headline invites judgment about right, wrong, fairness, or responsibility, and low when no normative evaluation is suggested; does not apply to normatively neutral events.

proposals.name: Visual scene vividness
proposals.rationale: Easily imagined scenes make headlines more attention-grabbing and memorable.
proposals.description: Scores high when the wording readily evokes a specific, imaginable scene, and low when it remains abstract; does not apply when no concrete scene is described.

proposals.name: Concrete specificity
proposals.rationale: Concrete details help readers form expectations about what opening the article will reveal.
proposals.description: Scores high when distinctive details, quantities, or actions anchor the story, and low when wording is generic; does not apply when specificity cannot be assessed from the headline.

proposals.name: Self-contained context
proposals.rationale: Context reduces the knowledge barrier that otherwise suppresses clicks.
proposals.description: Scores high when the headline explains enough background to understand why the event matters, and low when it depends on missing context; does not apply when context is unnecessary.

proposals.name: Direct reader address
proposals.rationale: Direct address converts a general story into an individually relevant prompt.
proposals.description: Scores high when the headline explicitly addresses readers or their choices, and low when it speaks only about others; does not apply without second-person or collective-reader language.

proposals.name: Conversational intimacy
proposals.rationale: Perceived conversational closeness can increase attention beyond subject matter alone.
proposals.description: Scores high when first-person voice, informal phrasing, or personal quotation creates closeness, and low when institutional language dominates; does not apply when voice is unavailable.

proposals.name: Social discussion potential
proposals.rationale: Conversation value can amplify readership even when standard news values are weak.
proposals.description: Scores high when the headline naturally invites sharing, debate, amusement, or conversation, and low when it offers little to discuss; does not apply when audience response cannot be inferred.

proposals.name: Constructive solution signal
proposals.rationale: Solution-oriented stories may attract readers seeking efficacy, hope, or lessons.
proposals.description: Scores high when the headline suggests recovery, remedy, adaptation, or constructive change, and low when it presents only a problem; does not apply without a discernible response or solution.

proposals.name: Individual agency
proposals.rationale: Intentional personal action creates a readable narrative independent of elite status or institutional action.
proposals.description: Scores high when a clearly identified person makes a consequential choice or takes purposeful action, and low when people are passive or absent; does not apply without meaningful human agency.

proposals.name: Explainer-question framing
proposals.parent: explainer format slot and homepage packaging
proposals.description: Headline is phrased as a direct “why,” “how,” or “can” question rather than as a declarative report.

proposals.name: Name-colon packaging
proposals.parent: profile or entertainment desk house style
proposals.description: Headline begins with a person’s name or role followed by a colon.

proposals.name: Quoted personal testimony
proposals.description: Headline contains a first-person quotation describing an individual’s experience or feeling.

proposals.name: Specialist acronym marker
proposals.description: Headline contains an unexplained acronym or initialism of three or more capital letters.

proposals.name: Country-first dateline syntax
proposals.description: Headline begins with a country, city, or region followed by an institutional action or event.

proposals.name: Numeral milestone wording
proposals.description: Headline includes a specific number tied to a count, age, date, term, or measured milestone.

proposals.name: Continuation or ordinal cue
proposals.parent: multi-day running story and sequence position
proposals.description: Headline uses words such as “second,” “again,” “back,” “after,” or “now” to signal a follow-up.

proposals.name: Obituary-label template
proposals.parent: obituary desk template and staffing workflow
proposals.description: Headline explicitly starts with “Obituary:” or uses a death-and-age formula.

proposals.name: Scare-quote styling
proposals.parent: house style or CMS formatting habit
proposals.description: Headline places a single word or short phrase in quotation marks without presenting a complete spoken sentence.

proposals.name: Compressed short headline
proposals.description: Headline contains seven or fewer words and omits an article, auxiliary verb, or other normally expected function word.

proposals.name: Curiosity Gap
proposals.rationale: Readers often click to resolve a clearly framed unanswered question or outcome.
proposals.description: clear setup but withholds the answer, outcome, or explanation; low when the headline fully resolves the story. Does not apply when wording is merely vague or incomprehensible

proposals.name: Immediate Comprehensibility
proposals.rationale: Instantly accessible meaning lowers cognitive friction and can increase clicks.
proposals.description: high when event and relevance are understandable on first reading; low when syntax, jargon, or missing context obstruct meaning. Does not apply when difficulty comes only from unfamiliar proper names

proposals.name: Everyday-Life Relevance
proposals.rationale: Everyday relevance can attract readers independently of conventional news values.
proposals.description: high when readers can map the story to ordinary routines, safety, money, family, or identity; low when it is remote or specialized. Does not apply when the headline offers no basis for judging relevance

proposals.name: Practical Utility
proposals.rationale: Actionable information gives readers a direct instrumental reason to open the article.
proposals.description: high when reading promises guidance for a decision, behavior, or situation; low when no action follows. Does not apply to purely descriptive stories with no implied decision

proposals.name: Concrete Visualizability
proposals.rationale: Vivid mental imagery can make a headline more attention-capturing and memorable.
proposals.description: high when wording depicts a specific, imaginable scene or action; low when it is abstract or bureaucratic. Does not apply when the headline provides too little detail to infer imagery

proposals.name: Protagonist Clarity
proposals.rationale: Clear roles reduce comprehension effort and help readers assess personal relevance.
proposals.description: high when readers can immediately identify who acts, experiences, or is affected; low when agents or roles are obscured. Does not apply to genuinely agentless events

proposals.name: Narrative Progression
proposals.rationale: Implied change over time creates a narrative reason to continue reading.
proposals.description: high when the headline implies a before-and-after, reversal, rescue, escalation, or ongoing arc; low when it states a static fact. Does not apply when no sequence is indicated

proposals.name: Outcome Uncertainty
proposals.rationale: Open consequential outcomes sustain suspense beyond the headline’s stated facts.
proposals.description: high when a consequential next step or resolution remains open; low when the result is settled. Does not apply when no meaningful outcome is implied

proposals.name: Perceived Contradiction
proposals.rationale: Contradiction creates a cognitive puzzle that can motivate opening the story.
proposals.description: high when the headline juxtaposes roles, expectations, or facts that seem incompatible; low when elements reinforce one another. Does not apply without a readable contrast

proposals.name: Emotional Immediacy
proposals.rationale: Explicit emotion can generate involvement not captured by topic categories alone.
proposals.description: high when wording conveys an explicit, intense, recognizable feeling or testimony; low when emotionally neutral. Does not apply when emotion is inferred only from the topic

proposals.name: Moral Judgment Trigger
proposals.rationale: Moral stakes invite readers to inspect facts, responsibility, and consequences.
proposals.description: high when the headline signals wrongdoing, injustice, hypocrisy, or redemption; low when it is normatively neutral. Does not apply when no conduct or norm is signaled

proposals.name: Referent Recognition
proposals.rationale: Recognizable referents increase immediate salience and reduce interpretive effort.
proposals.description: high when named people, institutions, places, or topics are likely recognizable to broad readers; low when referents are obscure. Does not apply when no identifying referent appears

proposals.name: Conversation Potential
proposals.rationale: Discussable stories can be clicked for opinion formation, empathy, or sharing.
proposals.description: high when the headline naturally invites opinion, argument, empathy, or sharing; low when it offers little to discuss. Does not apply when no stance, dilemma, or relatable hook is signaled

proposals.name: Credibility Framing
proposals.rationale: Attribution and evidence cues affect trust and willingness to investigate a claim.
proposals.description: high when a claim is attributed to an identifiable source or grounded in concrete evidence; low when unsupported or sensationalized. Does not apply to straightforward event reports

proposals.name: Playful Language
proposals.rationale: Entertainment value can motivate clicks independently of topic importance.
proposals.description: high when wording uses wit, irony, or playful phrasing; low when it is flat and literal. Does not apply when no tonal cue is present

proposals.name: Very short headline
proposals.description: Contains six or fewer whitespace-delimited words.

proposals.name: Genre-label prefix
proposals.parent: desk template and section house style
proposals.description: Begins with a capitalized label followed by a colon, such as “Obituary:” or “Analysis:”.

proposals.name: Interrogative lead
proposals.description: Begins with “Why”, “How”, “What”, or “Can” and frames the headline as a question or explanation.

proposals.name: Scare-quoted hook
proposals.description: Places a colloquial, evaluative, or slogan-like phrase in quotation marks rather than using only plain event wording.

proposals.name: First-person testimony
proposals.description: Contains a quoted first-person pronoun or possessive such as “my”, “I”, “we”, or “our”.

proposals.name: Named-public-figure lead
proposals.description: Leads with or centers a person’s proper name, title, or celebrity/sports identity rather than an anonymous actor.

proposals.name: Court-process formula
proposals.description: Uses a standard legal-status phrase such as “faces hearing”, “denies charge”, “on trial”, or “acquitted”.

proposals.name: Overseas place-name marker
proposals.description: Contains a named foreign country, city, region, or demonym as an explicit location marker.

proposals.name: Running-story sequence cue
proposals.description: Contains an ordinal or continuity cue such as “first”, “second”, “again”, “back”, “after”, or “now”, revealing follow-up position in an ongoing story.

proposals.name: Breaking-cycle verb
proposals.description: Uses a bare present-tense event construction such as “X votes”, “Y dies”, or “Z takes”, without a date or time phrase.

proposals.name: Curiosity Gap
proposals.rationale: Readers click when a headline leaves a concrete, answerable question unresolved.
proposals.description: high when the headline leaves a specific, answerable question unresolved; low when it states the outcome or offers no puzzle. Does not apply when no fact is withheld or sought

proposals.name: Personal Relevance
proposals.rationale: Directly personal stakes can attract clicks even when public institutions, scale, or celebrity are absent.
proposals.description: high when the headline addresses the reader’s choices, family, health, safety, or routine; low for distant impersonal events. Does not apply when no individual stake is evident

proposals.name: Practical Utility
proposals.rationale: Immediate usefulness motivates clicks independently of prestige, danger, or novelty.
proposals.description: high when the headline promises usable advice, instructions, or decision-relevant knowledge; low when it offers no practical takeaway. Does not apply when no action or decision is implied

proposals.name: Perceived Threat
proposals.rationale: Perceived personal risk heightens attention beyond generic crisis or violence cues.
proposals.description: high when it signals plausible personal bodily, financial, legal, or safety harm; low when stakes are remote or benign. Does not apply when no threatened loss is present

proposals.name: Emotional Arousal
proposals.rationale: Explicit affective intensity can drive readership even without human-interest narrative.
proposals.description: high when wording explicitly signals intense fear, grief, anger, joy, or shock; low when wording is emotionally neutral. Does not apply when no affective cue appears

proposals.name: Moral Transgression
proposals.rationale: Moral judgment attracts attention when wrongdoing is visible but not necessarily criminal or legal.
proposals.description: high when the headline depicts explicit abuse, deception, cruelty, or unfairness; low when conduct is normatively neutral. Does not apply when no conduct is presented for evaluation

proposals.name: Identity Resonance
proposals.rationale: Group identity can mobilize readers without domestic relevance or celebrity.
proposals.description: high when the headline explicitly invokes membership involving language, religion, nationality, gender, class, or culture; low without such cues. Does not apply when no group boundary is evident

proposals.name: Agent Conflict
proposals.rationale: Nonviolent opposition can create attention beyond crisis, violence, and legal signals.
proposals.description: high when two agents or sides clearly oppose, accuse, compete, or negotiate against one another; low for unilateral or cooperative action. Does not apply when no relational contest appears

proposals.name: State Change
proposals.rationale: Before-and-after structure gives readers a reason to learn the intervening story.
proposals.description: high when the headline shows a transition between conditions, roles, or statuses; low when it describes a static state. Does not apply without a before-and-after implication

proposals.name: Contextual Self-Sufficiency
proposals.rationale: Self-contained headlines lower comprehension costs for readers without prior story knowledge.
proposals.description: high when roles, places, or actions explain named references within the headline; low when bare names, acronyms, or allusions require prior knowledge. Does not apply when no potentially unfamiliar reference appears

proposals.name: Concrete Imagery
proposals.rationale: Visualizable scenes make headlines more engaging and memorable.
proposals.description: high when the headline describes a physical scene, object, or action that is easy to picture; low for abstract policy or assessment. Does not apply without depictable content

proposals.name: Plain-Language Clarity
proposals.rationale: Low processing effort increases the chance of immediate clicking.
proposals.description: high when grammar and wording are immediately understandable and unambiguous; low with jargon, compression, or unclear references. Does not apply when there is insufficient text to judge

proposals.name: Specificity
proposals.rationale: Bounded details signal an intelligible story rather than generic importance.
proposals.description: high when the headline supplies bounded details such as a number, location, object, or clear causal relation; low when claims are vague or generalized. Does not apply without a factual proposition

proposals.name: Credibility Cue
proposals.rationale: Attribution or evidence can make a claim seem worth checking.
proposals.description: high when the headline provides accountable attribution, evidence, data, study, or quotation; low for unsupported assertions. Does not apply to purely event-descriptive headlines

proposals.name: Conversation Potential
proposals.rationale: Discussion potential can amplify readership through disagreement, empathy, or social sharing.
proposals.description: high when the headline invites broad opinion, argument, empathy, or emotional reaction; low when it offers no social or evaluative angle. Does not apply without a proposition likely to prompt response

proposals.name: Headline length
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Count the headline’s whitespace-delimited words, ignoring punctuation. Treat unusually short or long headlines as the channel.

proposals.name: Question/explainer framing
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Mark headlines that are questions or begin with “why,” “how,” or “can.”

proposals.name: Boilerplate format label
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Mark explicit labels such as “Obituary:” or recurring package prefixes before the headline text.

proposals.name: First-person testimonial voice
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Mark first-person possessives or quoted personal testimony, such as “my,” “we,” or “being.”

proposals.name: Entity and acronym density
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Count capitalized names, initials, acronyms, and honorifics relative to total words.

proposals.name: Geographic routing markers
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Mark explicit country, city, regional, or demonym references, and record their geographic category.

proposals.name: Wire-style attribution
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Mark headlines ending in attribution formulas such as “says,” “scientist says,” or a named official’s title.

proposals.name: Continuation and ordinal cues
proposals.parent: position in a running story or package
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Mark words indicating sequence or follow-up, including “first,” “second,” “again,” “back,” “now,” or “after.”

proposals.name: Calendar-specific wording
proposals.parent: seasonal news cycle or publication timing
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Mark named seasons, holidays, years, or explicit calendar references such as “Christmas” or “21st Century.”

proposals.name: House punctuation conventions
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Record distinctive use of colons, quotation marks, hyphens, apostrophes, and question marks independent of their meaning.

proposals.name: Curiosity gap
proposals.rationale: Open loops create a direct information-seeking motive for readership.
proposals.description: High when the headline withholds a consequential answer while making a specific question apparent; low when it resolves or raises no question, and it does not apply without an implied answer. | DESCRIPTION: Distinct unanswered questions can motivate readers to click for closure.

proposals.name: Practical utility
proposals.rationale: Readers may click to obtain immediately usable advice.
proposals.description: High when the headline promises actionable guidance for a reader’s decision or behavior; low when it offers no usable takeaway, and it does not apply to purely descriptive reporting. | DESCRIPTION: Actionable usefulness can attract readers independently of news prominence.

proposals.name: Direct personal applicability
proposals.rationale: Personal consequences can drive clicks even without elite actors or major events.
proposals.description: High when information could affect ordinary readers’ immediate choices, routines, or safety; low when relevance is remote, and it does not apply when relevance requires a specialized role. | DESCRIPTION: Immediate applicability differs from geographic or national relevance.

proposals.name: Identity resonance
proposals.rationale: Group identification can increase attention and perceived self-relevance.
proposals.description: High when the headline invokes belonging, values, language, generation, or group experience; low when no identity cue appears, and it does not apply when identity is merely incidental. | DESCRIPTION: Identity-linked material may feel personally significant to readers.

proposals.name: Emotional arousal
proposals.rationale: Strong affect can prompt impulsive attention and clicking.
proposals.description: High when wording clearly evokes strong fear, anger, joy, disgust, or awe; low when emotionally neutral, and it does not apply when no affective response is signaled. | DESCRIPTION: Emotional intensity is separate from crisis, violence, or human-interest content.

proposals.name: Cross-claim conflict
proposals.rationale: Readers may click to assess which competing account is credible.
proposals.description: High when competing assertions, interpretations, or positions are explicit; low when only one claim is presented, and it does not apply to physical conflict alone. | DESCRIPTION: Intellectual or evidentiary disagreement can attract readers without institutional action.

proposals.name: Explanatory promise
proposals.rationale: Readers often seek understanding rather than merely event awareness.
proposals.description: High when the headline promises reasons, mechanisms, or implications through “why,” “how,” or equivalent wording; low for event-only updates, and it does not apply to rhetorical questions lacking explanation. | DESCRIPTION: Explanatory framing offers a distinct informational payoff.

proposals.name: Narrative tension
proposals.rationale: Incomplete story arcs encourage readers to discover what happens next.
proposals.description: High when an ongoing attempt, predicament, or process has an outcome withheld; low when the situation is fully settled, and it does not apply without an unfolding process. | DESCRIPTION: Ongoing narrative suspense can sustain reader attention independently of crisis severity.

proposals.name: Concrete specificity
proposals.rationale: Concrete titles reduce uncertainty about what clicking will deliver.
proposals.description: High when the headline supplies precise, distinctive details rather than generic abstractions; low when vague, and it does not apply when the subject cannot be described more specifically. | DESCRIPTION: Specific wording helps readers form an immediate mental model of the article.

proposals.name: Visualizability
proposals.rationale: Easily imagined scenes may capture attention in headline-heavy environments.
proposals.description: High when the wording depicts a scene, object, gesture, or physical action readily pictured; low when wholly abstract, and it does not apply to inherently nonvisual topics. | DESCRIPTION: Imagery can make a headline arresting without relying on novelty or celebrity.

proposals.name: Plain-language accessibility
proposals.rationale: Comprehension is a prerequisite for broad readership and clicking.
proposals.description: High when common words and straightforward syntax make the meaning instantly clear; low when jargon or dense construction impedes comprehension, and it does not apply when unavoidable technical language is central. | DESCRIPTION: Accessible phrasing expands the pool of readers who can understand the headline immediately.

proposals.name: Shareability
proposals.rationale: Discussion and sharing amplify article exposure and clicks.
proposals.description: High when the headline is self-contained, quotable, and easy to discuss or pass along; low when dependent on obscure context, and it does not apply to inherently private or personal material. | DESCRIPTION: A headline that travels socially can generate readership beyond its initial placement.

proposals.name: Positive agency
proposals.rationale: Stories of efficacy can invite identification, admiration, or hope-driven readership.
proposals.description: High when people or communities are shown helping, solving, resisting, or achieving; low when purely passive or deteriorating, and it does not apply without meaningful human response. | DESCRIPTION: Agency and constructive outcomes may attract readers differently from institutional action.

proposals.name: Cultural recognizability
proposals.rationale: Shared references lower interpretive effort and increase immediate relevance.
proposals.description: High when a widely familiar symbol, phrase, practice, or reference enables instant comprehension; low when obscure, and it does not apply when no cultural reference appears. | DESCRIPTION: Familiar cultural hooks can attract attention without requiring a celebrity subject.

proposals.name: Playful framing
proposals.rationale: Entertaining presentation may increase curiosity and voluntary engagement.
proposals.description: High when wit, irony, punning, or an entertaining metaphor makes the headline distinctive; low when strictly literal or bureaucratic, and it does not apply when levity would be inappropriate or absent. | DESCRIPTION: Tone can make an otherwise ordinary subject unusually clickable.

proposals.name: Headline length
proposals.description: Count the headline’s words, ignoring punctuation.

proposals.name: Interrogative framing
proposals.description: Mark headlines beginning with “Why”, “How”, “Can”, or another direct question form.

proposals.name: Quoted wording
proposals.description: Mark headlines containing quotation marks around a phrase or speaker’s words.

proposals.name: Numeric specificity
proposals.description: Mark headlines containing numerals, ages, dates, counts, percentages, or monetary amounts.

proposals.name: Article-type label
proposals.description: Mark explicit labels such as “Obituary” or similarly templated format markers.

proposals.name: First-person testimony
proposals.description: Mark headlines using “I”, “my”, or an individualized first-person account.

proposals.name: Follow-up wording
proposals.description: Mark terms such as “again”, “back”, “second”, “still”, or “now” that imply continuation.

proposals.name: Ordinal or milestone wording
proposals.parent: story position within a running news cycle
proposals.description: Mark “first”, “third”, “100 million”, or other wording signaling sequence or milestone status.

proposals.name: Proper-name prominence
proposals.description: Mark headlines led by a named person, organization, or place rather than an event description.

proposals.name: Domestic-geography marker
proposals.parent: domestic desk allocation and audience targeting
proposals.description: Mark explicit references to the UK, Britain, or a UK-specific institution.

proposals.name: Clickbait or curiosity framing
proposals.rationale: Readers click to resolve curiosity gaps, driving high same-outlet traffic despite low news value.
proposals.description: Headlines that start with "Why", "How", or use punctuation to tease a counterintuitive premise score high; straightforward factual reports score low.

proposals.name: Paradoxical or incongruous juxtaposition
proposals.rationale: Oddities trigger high reader curiosity, generating viral clicks irrespective of traditional news weight.
proposals.description: High score if headline combines two unexpected concepts (e.g., destroying wine, salt in tea). Standard narratives score low.

proposals.name: Domestic pop-culture or entertainment references
proposals.rationale: Readers often seek light entertainment, driving massive clicks that standard hard-news criteria miss.
proposals.description: Scores high for local celebrity gossip, reality TV, or sports drama; scores low for foreign or elite political news.

proposals.name: Direct first-person or quoted narrative
proposals.rationale: Personal, emotional narratives drive high reader empathy and relatability, prompting frequent clicks.
proposals.description: Headlines using "I", "Me", or "My" score high. Third-person institutional reports score low.

proposals.name: UK-centric cultural or local hook
proposals.rationale: BBC's primarily domestic audience clicks heavily on hyper-local or culturally familiar soft news.
proposals.description: Scores high if mentioning UK entities (e.g., Wetherspoons); scores low for foreign equivalents without domestic ties.

proposals.name: Provocative or emotional adjectives
proposals.rationale: Emotional intensity hooks reader attention, elevating clicks beyond what standard structural news values predict.
proposals.description: High score for highly evocative words (e.g., macabre, unbearable, catastrophe). Neutral reporting scores low.

proposals.name: Technological or scientific explainers
proposals.rationale: Practical utility and shareable facts generate high reader engagement and forwarding.
proposals.description: Scores high for accessible "how-to" or quirky science. Pure academic research without daily application scores low.

proposals.name: Geopolitical violence without domestic stakes
proposals.rationale: Clicks reflect a domestic bias; readers often ignore distant crises lacking recognizable elite actors.
proposals.description: Foreign war updates without UK/US involvement score low. High-stakes domestic conflicts score high.

proposals.name: Explicit high economic magnitudes
proposals.rationale: Concrete, massive numbers provide immediate scale and shock value, heavily driving reader clicks.
proposals.description: High score if headline highlights massive explicit costs or physical quantities. Vague institutional changes score low.

proposals.name: Domestic political process explainers
proposals.rationale: Confused readers actively seek systemic explainers, creating intense traffic spikes distinct from breaking news.
proposals.description: High score for explaining domestic systems (e.g., US/UK elections). Scores low for breaking foreign political results.

proposals.name: Heavy human-interest overcome adversity
proposals.rationale: Inspiring or shocking personal sagars compel high engagement, bypassing standard hard-news prioritization.
proposals.description: High score for extreme personal redemption or survival stories. Routine institutional updates score low.

proposals.name: Headline-led stark visual imagery
proposals.rationale: Visually evocative prompts mentally stimulate the reader, strongly predicting a click.
proposals.description: High score for vivid, cinematic scenes (e.g., coal tip, heavy losses). Abstract policies score low.

proposals.name: Outlier magnitude or numeric thresholds
proposals.rationale: Large quantities signal immediate scale, attracting clicks for seemingly massive events.
proposals.description: Scores high if explicit numbers denote extreme scale (e.g., 100 million, 99 years). Missing or small numbers score low.

proposals.name: Systemic or institutional mystery
proposals.rationale: Unanswered systemic questions drive readers to click for closure more than definitive institutional actions.
proposals.description: High score for interrogating systemic rules (e.g., Archie's title). Clear-cut legal verdicts score low.

proposals.name: Unusual animal or ecological angle
proposals.rationale: Quirky nature stories offer highly shareable soft news, driving viral traffic invisible to elite-actor models.
proposals.description: High score for bizarre animal behaviors; standard climate reports score low.

proposals.name: SOFT-NEWS-FRONTING
proposals.parent: Editorial placement in designated click-magnet slots or soft-news promotional pushes
proposals.description: Headline uses a non-urgent conversational hook, listicle framing, or curiosity gap (e.g., "Why...", "How...") to draw clicks.

proposals.name: CELEBRITY-OBIT-VERB
proposals.parent: Rapid editorial mobilization for pre-written, highly anticipated celebrity deaths
proposals.description: Headline explicitly states the death of an actor, musician, or pop-culture figure using obituary markers.

proposals.name: DOMESTIC-VS-FOREIGN-SYNTAX
proposals.parent: Proximity bias and varying editorial desk resources between domestic and foreign beats
proposals.description: Headline follows terse, immediate syntax for domestic/visual events (e.g., "Russian jet shot down") but uses summarizing syntax for foreign events (e.g., "Chad army snubs...").

proposals.name: CLICKBAIT-SCARE-QUOTE
proposals.parent: House-style formatting for optimized reader-engagement features and explainers
proposals.description: Headline features a prominent first-person quote or provocative phrase enclosed in single quotation marks to tease the article.

proposals.name: SOFT-NEWS-PERSONA
proposals.parent: High production-investment in specific human-interest or feature packages
proposals.description: Headline highlights a specific ordinary citizen's unexpected juxtaposition of traits (e.g., "shot, left for dead, now a...").

proposals.name: ANGLO-CELEBRITY-MARKER
proposals.parent: Inclusion of clickable UK-centric cultural topics over international hard news
proposals.description: Headline names an entertainer, athlete, or reality star highly recognized in the domestic UK market.

proposals.name: RESTRICTED-CONTEXT-BREVITY
proposals.parent: Placement as an urgent breaking-news ticker on the homepage, relying on visual urgency rather than textual explanation
proposals.description: Headline consists of a very short, ambiguous noun phrase lacking full context (e.g., "Mariupol 'near to catastrophe'").

proposals.name: SCIENCE-ADVICE-VERB
proposals.parent: Lifestyle desk producing evergreen, highly shareable web content
proposals.description: Headline features an instructive or authoritative verb directing personal action or revealing a surprising fact (e.g., "Add salt...").

proposals.name: HARD-NEWS-CONTINUITY
proposals.parent: Multi-day running stories that accumulate reader familiarity but lack fresh domestic hooks
proposals.description: Headline updates an ongoing international political event using non-final actions (e.g., "strike deal", "vows elections", "faces hearing").

proposals.name: SHARED-NARRATIVE-FRAMING
proposals.parent: Efforts by editors to boost click-through rates for complex topics by piggybacking on highly searched cultural keywords
proposals.description: Headline references famous media properties or royalty to frame a relatively obscure legal or social issue.

proposals.name: Emotional Trigger Words
proposals.rationale: Strong emotive language taps into affective responses that drive high click-through rates.
proposals.description: Headlines containing visceral emotional adjectives (e.g., 'worst', 'unbearable', 'anger') score 1; purely factual headlines score 0. Does not apply to neutral headlines.

proposals.name: Clickbait Teasers
proposals.rationale: Directly addresses the reader's curiosity, a powerful driver of reader engagement independent of topic.
proposals.description: Headlines using hook phrases like 'Why we...', 'How you...', or 'What we...' score 1; declarative headlines score 0.

proposals.name: Counter-Intuitive Claims
proposals.rationale: Cognitive dissonance strongly provokes reader curiosity and subsequent article clicks.
proposals.description: Headlines presenting absurd or paradoxical concepts (e.g., 'add salt to tea') score 1; expected scenarios score 0.

proposals.name: Explicit Monetary Values
proposals.rationale: Concrete numerical anchors make economic or financial impact stories more tangible and clickable.
proposals.description: Headlines featuring explicit currency symbols or large numbers (e.g., '€200m') score 1; headlines without specific financial figures score 0.

proposals.name: High-Recognition Celebrity
proposals.rationale: Parasocial interest in truly recognizable global names drives clicks beyond general entertainment value.
proposals.description: Headlines naming globally iconic figures (e.g., Betty White, Ariana Grande) score 1; niche public figures or officials score 0.

proposals.name: UK Domestic Colloquialisms
proposals.rationale: The BBC's core domestic audience clicks heavily on hyper-local, culturally resonant content.
proposals.description: Headlines featuring British cultural markers (e.g., 'Wetherspoons') score 1; formal international news or generic nouns score 0.

proposals.name: Geopolitical Power Confrontation
proposals.rationale: Imminent large-scale conflict or great-power friction is a massive driver of global readership.
proposals.description: Headlines explicitly naming a major power (US, China, Russia) alongside conflict words (war, shot, losses) score 1; domestic politics score 0.

proposals.name: Second-Person Direct Address
proposals.rationale: Personalization makes abstract news feel immediately relevant, significantly increasing click likelihood.
proposals.description: Headlines using the pronoun 'you' or 'we' to speak directly to the reader score 1; third-person narratives score 0.

proposals.name: Macro Health Statistics
proposals.rationale: Concrete quantitative milestones provide clear, clickable anchors for tracking major ongoing crises.
proposals.description: Headlines containing large-scale numerical milestones (e.g., '100 million doses') score 1; qualitative policy descriptions score 0.

proposals.name: Royal Family Whodunit
proposals.rationale: Gossip or mystery framed as an analytical question highly incentivizes readers to click.
proposals.description: Headlines phrasing royal family news as an explanatory question (e.g., 'Why is Archie...') score 1; straightforward royal reports score 0.

proposals.name: Bizarre Animal Hook
proposals.rationale: Quirky, easily visualized oddities provide highly shareable soft news that readers click for entertainment.
proposals.description: Headlines featuring animals in unnatural or quirky scenarios (e.g., hermit crabs 'wearing' plastic) score 1; standard nature reports score 0.

proposals.name: Unusual Occupation Mix
proposals.rationale: Juxtaposing the mundane with the extraordinary creates a highly clickable David-vs-Goliath narrative.
proposals.description: Headlines juxtaposing a mundane job with extreme violence or sports (e.g., schoolteacher fighting Pacquiao) score 1; standard career reports score 0.

proposals.name: Cultural Trends Analysis
proposals.rationale: Readers click trend pieces to validate their own changing worldviews or personal experiences.
proposals.description: Headlines analyzing broad societal shifts or global preferences (e.g., 'Why the world now loves...') score 1; isolated event reports score 0.

proposals.name: Named Foreign Capitals
proposals.rationale: Foreign news lacking immediate domestic relevance often struggles to attract casual reader clicks.
proposals.description: Headlines naming specific foreign countries or capitals (e.g., Chad, Ivory Coast) without major power involvement score 0; globally recognized regions score 1.

proposals.name: Inverted Quirky Celebrity
proposals.rationale: Eccentric phrasing implies a highly readable, bizarre narrative that converts to clicks.
proposals.description: Headlines using scare quotes for eccentric behavior or quotes (e.g., 'Magic owls') score 1; straightforward political reports score 0.

proposals.name: FORMATTING QUOTES
proposals.description: Presence of quotation marks | DESCRIPTION: Headline contains scare quotes or quoted speech, a textual fingerprint of soft news, interviews, orreaction stories that editors push as feature content.

proposals.name: EXPLAINER HEADLINE
proposals.description: Starts with interrogative or how-to | DESCRIPTION: Headline begins with 'How', 'Why', 'Can', or 'What', functioning as an explanatory or analytical piece rather than hard breaking news.

proposals.name: CELEBRITY OBITUARY
proposals.description: Names deceased famous person | DESCRIPTION: Headline explicitly mentions the death of an actor, musician, or public entertainer, triggering immediate high-volume reader searches.

proposals.name: EVERGREEN SOFT NEWS
proposals.parent: Slow news day or 'And Finally' beat
proposals.description: Fluff, animals, or quirky science | DESCRIPTION: Headline focuses on animals, food, or oddity (e.g., tea, hermit crabs, dinosaurs) capturing non-political readers but lacking immediate news merit.

proposals.name: DOMESTIC LEGAL CRIME
proposals.description: UK police or court phrasing | DESCRIPTION: Headline uses UK-specific justice boilerplate like 'denies affray', 'remanded', or 'court hearing' absent international war context.

proposals.name: FOREIGN POWER-SHARING
proposals.description: African or Middle East coups | DESCRIPTION: Headline mentions distant institutional actions like 'power-sharing', 'rebels', or specific coup leaders, carrying a formal diplomatic tone.

proposals.name: SOFT HUMAN INTEREST
proposals.description: Personal triumph or suffering | DESCRIPTION: Headline centers on an anonymous individual's trauma, recovery, or personal mission using emotional framing rather than named elite actors.

proposals.name: SUPERLATIVE FRAMING
proposals.description: Uses absolute or extreme terms | DESCRIPTION: Headline contains extreme modifiers like 'worst', 'unbearable', 'perfect', or '100 million', maximizing emotional arousal to drive clicks.

proposals.name: BIOPIC OR DOCS
proposals.description: Mentions films, TV, or media | DESCRIPTION: Headline references a documentary, biopic, or pop-culture media property, leveraging search trends rather than intrinsic news weight.

proposals.name: PARLIAMENTARY CRISIS
proposals.description: Mentions specific institutional bills | DESCRIPTION: Headline focuses on domestic parliamentary procedure or elections (e.g., 'covid app', 'defence chief'), heavily covered but narrowly framed.

proposals.name: Unusual juxtaposition of hard and soft concepts
proposals.rationale: High cognitive dissonance or ironic contrasts strongly drive reader curiosity and virality.
proposals.description: Scores high if the headline explicitly pairs a high-stakes, dangerous, or institutional concept (e.g., crime, war, politics) with a mundane, soft, or domestic concept (e.g., teaching, youth centre, tea). Scores low if topics are purely hard or soft.

proposals.name: Poses an explicit or implicit question
proposals.rationale: Information gaps provoke high curiosity, driving readers to click to resolve the mystery.
proposals.description: Scores high if the syntax forms a direct question, uses scare quotes to challenge a concept, or teases a hidden explanation. Scores low if the headline is a declarative statement of fact.

proposals.name: Distinct pop culture or media reference
proposals.rationale: Popular culture taps into pre-existing audience interests, driving higher traffic than abstract news.
proposals.description: Scores high if the text explicitly references a well-known movie, song, TV show, or celebrity. Scores low if restricted to obscure figures or institutional roles.

proposals.name: Embedded first-person human interest
proposals.rationale: Emotional testimony and personal voices increase reader empathy and click-through rates.
proposals.description: Scores high if the text uses first-person pronouns or quotation marks to highlight a relatable personal experience. Scores low for detached, institutional reporting.

proposals.name: Micro-level framing of macro events
proposals.rationale: Readers frequently click to read about personal narratives rather than abstract geopolitical concepts.
proposals.description: Scores high if it focuses on a single individual's narrative (e.g., "Son of Russian spies") rather than broad geopolitical outcomes. Scores low for general institutional actions.

proposals.name: Presence of quirky or novelty concepts
proposals.rationale: Novelty, weird trivia, and lighter "watercooler" facts generate high shares and casual clicks.
proposals.description: Scores high if the text features unusual animals, bizarre historical facts, or surprising scientific claims. Scores low for routine political or crime stories.

proposals.name: Direct conflict between prominent actors
proposals.rationale: Interpersonal drama and direct clashes between prominent figures trigger immediate reader engagement.
proposals.description: Scores high if the headline depicts explicit, active friction between named elite actors. Scores low for passive institutions or systemic policy changes.

proposals.name: Subversion of authority or expectations
proposals.rationale: Audiences are drawn to stories that subvert expectations or challenge institutional norms.
proposals.description: Scores high if the text highlights irony, rebellion, or the breaking of norms. Scores low if it straightforwardly reports an institutional process.

proposals.name: Explicit emotional valuation words
proposals.rationale: Strong emotional triggers in text reliably convert passing page-scrollers into actual readers.
proposals.description: Scores high if the text uses vivid adjectives indicating extreme emotion or shock. Scores low for neutral, procedural language regarding legal or political events.

proposals.name: Resolving a recognized global running story
proposals.rationale: Readers click on updates to stories they are already following and emotionally invested in.
proposals.description: Scores high if it names a recent major crisis (e.g., Covid, Mariupol). Scores low for isolated foreign events lacking immediate context.

proposals.name: Quantified scale or numbers
proposals.rationale: Specific numbers ground a story, making abstract events tangible and highly clickable.
proposals.description: Scores high if specific numbers, ages, or financial sums are included. Scores low for unquantified, general statements.

proposals.name: Generic political or legal procedure
proposals.rationale: Procedural updates are often viewed as dull by general readers, reducing click-through.
proposals.description: Scores low if the text highlights routine bureaucracy, court dates, or elections without notable elite names. Scores high if featuring a major reversal.

proposals.name: Proximity to domestic (UK) audience
proposals.rationale: Readers strongly prefer news that directly impacts or relates to their immediate environment.
proposals.description: Scores high if the headline mentions local places, UK figures, or highly domestic issues. Scores low for distant foreign events lacking a UK hook.

proposals.name: High-consequence catastrophic framing
proposals.rationale: Imminent doom and existential stakes naturally provoke high anxiety and urgent clicking.
proposals.description: Scores high if the text explicitly predicts disaster or severe irreversible consequences. Scores low for tentative or standard political friction.

proposals.name: Definitive marker of an obituary
proposals.rationale: Morbidity and closure regarding famous figures are highly reliable drivers of immediate reader traffic.
proposals.description: Scores high if the text explicitly uses "dies", "obituary", or "killed". Scores low for tangential celebrity references.

proposals.name: CURIOUSTY-GAP FORMAT
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Headline poses a direct question or teases a counterintuitive revelation designed to compel a click to resolve the ambiguity.

proposals.name: LISTICLE-STYLE PROMISE
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Headline contains a phrase like 'What we can learn', 'How you can', or implies a step-by-step guide.

proposals.name: NAMED CELEBRITY DEATH
proposals.parent: standing editorial workflow for celebrity deaths
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Uses the word 'dies', 'dead', or 'obituary' alongside a recognizable celebrity name, prompting immediate high-traffic nostalgia clicks.

proposals.name: EVERYDAY MYSTERY OR QUIRK
proposals.parent: social media virality and human interest desk
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Features a bizarre but low-stakes topic, such as adding salt to tea, which drives massive sharing and debate.

proposals.name: BRITISH ROYALTY MENTION
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Headline explicitly names a royal title or family member, heavily boosting UK-centric traffic regardless of political importance.

proposals.name: DOMESTIC POLITICIANS IN SOFT-NEWS
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Features a national politician in an uncharacteristic or lifestyle scenario, bridging hard and soft news audiences.

proposals.name: LOCAL HOOK WITH GLOBAL SCOPE
proposals.parent: editorial policy of localizing global events
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Mentions a domestic entity (e.g., UK app, French scientists) in an international or scientific story to drive home clicks.

proposals.name: OUTLET-SPECIFIC OBITUARY TAG
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Contains the specific prefix 'Obituary:' marking a standardized editorial format that draws a specific reader demographic.

proposals.name: COMMON-WORD ENTITIES
proposals.parent: human interest and lifestyle beat focus
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Focuses on animals, food, or nature rather than named geopolitical entities, appealing to casual scrollers rather than hard-news readers.

proposals.name: SUPERLATIVE OR RECORD MARKER
proposals.description: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Contains words like 'first', 'most', 'giant', or numbers implying a record-breaking scale to inflate perceived importance.

proposals.name: Explicit absolute or comparative numbers
proposals.rationale: Numbers promise concrete, verifiable takeaways, driving higher click-through rates.
proposals.description: Headline contains at least one hard numeric figure, number of casualties, monetary sum, or explicitly quantifies an outcome; low if no numbers are present.

proposals.name: Quoted first-person speech
proposals.rationale: First-person quotes simulate emotional intimacy and voyeurism, directly engaging readers.
proposals.description: Headline contains text in quotation marks spoken by an everyday individual expressing a subjective feeling or personal experience; low for unquoted statements.

proposals.name: Geographic or physical dichotomy
proposals.rationale: Unexpected geographic combinations leverage cognitive novelty to capture reader curiosity.
proposals.description: Highlights a stark contrast between an unlikely location and a familiar concept, or juxtaposes two distinct places (e.g., French scientists, Mongolian sumo).

proposals.name: Bizarre or counter-intuitive action
proposals.rationale: Readers click to resolve the cognitive dissonance created by a paradoxical premise.
proposals.description: Features an action that violates common sense or logic, or explicitly contrasts two opposing concepts (e.g., spending money to destroy wine).

proposals.name: Unanswered explanatory premise
proposals.rationale: The information gap theory predicts users click to resolve the tension of an unanswered question.
proposals.description: Poses an explicit question, or starts with an interrogative word like 'Why' or 'How', demanding the reader click to find the answer.

proposals.name: Elite figure in personal conflict
proposals.rationale: Voyeuristic interest in the private lives of famous individuals drives high readership.
proposals.description: Mentions a widely recognized celebrity, elite actor, or royal figure embroiled in a personal, family, or health crisis rather than institutional action.

proposals.name: Pop-culture or entertainment reference
proposals.rationale: Entertainment news has massive, built-in audiences that reliably click on familiar names.
proposals.description: Headline contains the name of a well-known entertainer, pop-culture franchise, or sports star outside of standard match-report contexts.

proposals.name: Long-term temporal narrative framing
proposals.rationale: Narrative arcs promising a satisfying long-form character transformation attract readers.
proposals.description: Uses explicit phrasing indicating a prolonged struggle, delayed justice, or life transition spanning years (e.g., '17-year fight', 'now loves').

proposals.name: Explicit named collective identity
proposals.rationale: Readers often click to see how issues impact distinct or niche communities.
proposals.description: Focuses on an identifiable social group or demographic facing a localized issue (e.g., hermit crabs, French scientists, a specific village).

proposals.name: Unresolved mystery or ambiguity
proposals.rationale: Ambiguity creates a compelling puzzle that readers want to solve by reading the article.
proposals.description: Uses terms like 'vanished', 'mystery', or 'ghost' without immediately identifying the culprit or explaining the phenomenon in the text.

proposals.name: High-stakes elite conflict
proposals.rationale: High-stakes geopolitical tension induces anxiety-clicking to assess personal threat levels.
proposals.description: Features explicit threats of severe consequences between major powers or institutions (e.g., war, nuclear strikes, disaster).

proposals.name: Colloquialism alongside institutional actor
proposals.rationale: Translating dry political news into accessible language broadens the clicking audience.
proposals.description: Juxtaposes an informal, everyday term or slang with a formal institution, official, or politician (e.g., 'tricky Myanmar trip').

proposals.name: Intimate personal survival outcome
proposals.rationale: Sympathy and emotional resonance drive readers to engage with human suffering.
proposals.description: Depicts a vulnerable subject (mother, baby, 'vanished' husband) who escaped death or is enduring severe hardship; low for purely statistical harm.

proposals.name: Juxtaposition of opposing roles
proposals.rationale: Underdog narratives and surprising dualities exploit reader love for dramatic contrasts.
proposals.description: Headline structure explicitly contrasts two divergent identities or roles for one subject (e.g., schoolteacher fighting Pacquiao).

proposals.name: Everyday micro-issue with macro-claim
proposals.rationale: Soft news thrives on novelty, prompting clicks by making the unfamiliar relatable.
proposals.description: Applies a familiar, mundane activity or object (tea, owls, plastic) to a surprising or extraordinary context; low for strictly hard news.

proposals.name: Exotic locale beat marker
proposals.description: Headline features an article about a specific foreign country (e.g., Guinea, Chad, Mongolia) or regional niche (Amazon, Ivory Coast) that is not a major geopolitical focus.

proposals.name: Verbal human-interest framing
proposals.description: Headline relies heavily on scare quotes, first-person pronouns ('I', 'my', 'we'), or dramatic narrative phrasing ('vanished', 'murderer', 'high-flyer').

proposals.name: Explicit extreme emotion label
proposals.description: Headline uses overt emotional or evaluative words to describe the situation, such as 'disaster', 'catastrophe', 'unbearable', 'tricky', or 'anger'.

proposals.name: Episodic micro-narrative
proposals.description: Headline focuses entirely on a single named individual's localized plight (e.g., a mother, a schoolteacher, a widow) rather than broader institutional impact.

proposals.name: Unexplained opaque identifier
proposals.description: Headline contains names, locations, or acronyms with high assumed knowledge and no descriptive context (e.g., Mariupol, Gbagbo, ICC).

proposals.name: Analytical explainer framing
proposals.description: Headline is framed as a question or starts with analytical cues ('Why', 'How you can', 'What we can') indicating an evergreen or background context piece.

proposals.name: Human-vs-human combat terms
proposals.description: Headline mentions active warfare, explicit military hardware (jet, F-16), or direct human combat terms (shot, destroying, strikes).

proposals.name: Celebrity death boilerplate
proposals.description: Headline uses standard formulaic obituary structures, such as starting with 'Obituary:' or ending with 'dies aged [Number]'.

proposals.name: Oddity or novelty hook
proposals.description: Headline emphasizes a quirky, bizarre, or counterintuitive concept (e.g., adding salt to tea, magic owls, hermit crabs wearing plastic).

proposals.name: Narrative contrast syntax
proposals.description: Headline uses syntax to juxtapose a dark past with a redemptive present (e.g., 'Shot... now a', 'The murderer who's opening').
